definition: Cheerfully hopeful, especially when things look difficult.
examples: Despite the weak sales figures, the founder remained sanguine about the company's future.
Economists are less sanguine than the minister about a quick recovery.

definition: Involving or eager for a great deal of bloodshed.
examples: The sanguinary battle left thousands dead on both sides of the river.
Historians remember him as a sanguinary ruler who executed his rivals.

definition: Willing to act dishonestly in return for money; open to bribery.
examples: The venal official approved the permit only after receiving a payment.
Voters grew tired of a venal administration that sold favours to the highest bidder.

definition: Describing a fault that is minor and easily forgiven.
examples: Arriving five minutes late was a venial offence that nobody mentioned.
She treated his forgetfulness as a venial fault rather than a betrayal.

definition: To criticise or scold someone severely.
examples: The coach castigated the team for its careless defending in the second half.
Newspapers castigated the government over its slow response to the floods.

definition: To condemn someone or something in extremely harsh terms.
examples: The reviewer excoriated the film as lazy, dishonest and an insult to its audience.
In her speech she excoriated the bank for misleading its customers.

definition: To tell someone off sharply for something they have done wrong.
examples: The teacher upbraided the students for copying each other's work.
He upbraided himself for missing such an obvious error in the final report.

definition: Using very few words to say something.
examples: His laconic reply, a single 'no', ended the discussion before it had begun.
The report was laconic, covering a year of work in two paragraphs.

definition: Quiet by nature and reluctant to talk.
examples: The taciturn farmer answered most questions with a nod and rarely spoke a full sentence.
She was taciturn at meetings but wrote long, thoughtful emails afterwards.

definition: Fond of talking and inclined to talk a lot.
examples: The loquacious taxi driver told us his life story before we reached the airport.
Normally loquacious, he fell silent when the results were announced.

definition: Talking too much, especially about unimportant things.
examples: A garrulous neighbour kept her at the gate for half an hour.
The lecture was spoiled by a garrulous host who rambled through every introduction.

definition: Lasting for only a very short time.
examples: Fame on social media is ephemeral; last month's star is forgotten today.
The desert flowers are ephemeral, blooming for a few days after rain.

definition: Passing quickly or staying only briefly; not permanent.
examples: The drug's side effects were mild and transient, fading within an hour or two.
The town has a transient population of seasonal workers who leave after the harvest.

definition: Spending money or resources freely and wastefully.
examples: His prodigal spending on parties and cars emptied the inheritance within two years.
The city was prodigal with water until the reservoirs ran low.

definition: Remarkably great in size, amount or ability.
examples: She has a prodigious memory and can recite whole chapters.
Building the dam required a prodigious amount of concrete, more than any earlier project.

definition: Clever and inventive in a new or original way.
examples: The engineers found an ingenious way to cool the building without electricity.
It was an ingenious plan that used the rival's own rules against them.

definition: Innocent, trusting and openly honest, often to the point of being naive.
examples: His ingenuous questions revealed that he had never dealt with lawyers before.
She gave an ingenuous smile, unaware that she was being tricked.

definition: Not influenced by personal advantage; impartial.
examples: A dispute like this needs a disinterested judge with no stake in the outcome.
Her advice was disinterested, since she gained nothing whichever option we chose.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation; deliberately unclear.
examples: The minister gave an equivocal answer that satisfied neither side.
Results from the first trial were equivocal, so a second study was planned.

definition: To speak vaguely so as to avoid giving a clear answer.
examples: Asked directly about the layoffs, the manager equivocated and talked about market conditions instead.
Stop equivocating and tell us whether you support the proposal.

definition: Having mixed or opposing feelings about something.
examples: She felt ambivalent about the promotion, which paid more but meant moving away.
Voters remain ambivalent about the reform, liking its aims but doubting its cost.

definition: To make something bad less severe or less harmful.
examples: Planting trees along the river helped mitigate the flooding in the villages downstream.
The apology did little to mitigate the damage to his reputation.

definition: To make a bad situation better.
examples: New housing was built to ameliorate conditions in the crowded district.
The medicine ameliorated her symptoms but did not cure the disease.

definition: To make a problem or bad situation worse.
examples: Cutting the bus service will only exacerbate traffic in the city centre.
Stress at work exacerbated his headaches, which eased whenever he took a holiday.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or soften one's attitude.
examples: The landlord remained obdurate and would not lower the rent.
Even faced with clear evidence, the obdurate witness stuck to his story.

definition: Unwilling to compromise or to change a position.
examples: Talks collapsed because both parties were intransigent on wages and refused any middle figure.
The intransigent committee rejected every amendment, however small, that the members proposed.

definition: Dealing with things sensibly and practically rather than by theory or ideals.
examples: She took a pragmatic approach and fixed the cheapest problems first.
A pragmatic leader, he worked with anyone who could get results.

definition: Insisting that one's beliefs are certainly true and refusing to consider other views.
examples: He was so dogmatic about his diet that he lectured everyone at dinner.
Science advances when researchers are curious rather than dogmatic about what they already believe.

definition: To drain someone of energy or strength.
examples: The heat and humidity enervated the hikers, who could barely walk by midday.
Months of night shifts had enervated her so completely that she slept through weekends.

definition: To give energy, strength or new life to someone or something.
examples: A swim in the cold lake invigorated him, and he felt ready to work again.
The new director invigorated a department that had drifted for years.

definition: To praise someone or something highly, especially in public.
examples: Critics lauded the novel for its honesty, and it won three major prizes.
The mayor lauded the volunteers who had rebuilt the school.

definition: To praise something or someone with great enthusiasm.
examples: The brochure extols the benefits of mountain air, calling it a cure for every illness.
He extolled his mentor's patience in every interview, crediting her for his success.

definition: To speak about someone or something as being of little worth.
examples: He disparaged his rival's research as mere guesswork that no serious scientist would trust.
It is easy to disparage popular music, but writing a good song is hard.

definition: To unfairly attack the reputation or value of someone or something.
examples: The campaign tried to denigrate the candidate by spreading rumours.
She refused to denigrate her former colleagues, whatever she thought of them.

definition: Having or showing deep knowledge gained from study.
examples: The erudite professor quoted from memory in four languages during a single lecture.
Her erudite essay traced the idea back to ancient Greece.

definition: Too concerned with small details or formal rules, especially in showing off learning.
examples: His pedantic corrections of every comma annoyed the whole team.
It may sound pedantic, but the two terms do not mean the same thing.

definition: Understood by or meant for only a small group with special knowledge.
examples: The lecture was full of esoteric references that only specialists followed.
He collects esoteric facts about medieval coinage that only a handful of historians know.

definition: Known or understood by very few people; mysterious.
examples: The tax code is full of arcane rules that confuse even accountants.
She learned the arcane rituals of the old guild, which outsiders were never shown.

definition: Difficult to understand because it is complex or highly abstract.
examples: The philosopher's abstruse arguments lost most of the audience within the first ten minutes.
He has a gift for explaining abstruse mathematics in plain language.

definition: Clearly expressed and easy to understand.
examples: Her lucid explanation made the theory seem simple even to complete beginners.
The guide is short, lucid and free of jargon, so anyone can follow it.

definition: To make something unclear or hard to understand, often on purpose.
examples: The company used technical jargon to obfuscate the real cost.
Long footnotes obfuscated what should have been a simple point.

definition: Changing mood or behaviour suddenly and without good reason.
examples: The capricious manager praised a plan on Monday and cancelled it on Tuesday.
Mountain weather is capricious, so carry a jacket even on a sunny day.

definition: Having moods or opinions that change quickly and unpredictably.
examples: The mercurial striker could win a match or be sent off in the first ten minutes.
Working for such a mercurial boss kept everyone on edge.

definition: Very attentive to detail and hard to please, especially about cleanliness or accuracy.
examples: He is fastidious about his desk, with every pen in its place.
A fastidious editor, she checked each date against the original source.

definition: Extremely careful and precise about every detail.
examples: The detective kept meticulous notes on every interview, recording even the exact times.
Restoring the painting took two years of meticulous work with brushes of a single hair.

definition: Ordinary and unimaginative; lacking anything poetic or exciting.
examples: The mystery of the flickering lights had a prosaic explanation: a faulty switch.
After a year of adventure at sea, his prosaic office job felt unbearably dull.

definition: So ordinary and unoriginal that it is boring.
examples: The speech was a string of banal remarks about teamwork.
What began as a fresh idea became banal through endless repetition.

definition: Something that differs from what is normal or expected.
examples: A snowstorm in May is an anomaly in this region.
The auditors flagged several anomalies in the accounts, including payments with no matching invoices.

definition: A very small amount of something; a shortage.
examples: The study was limited by a paucity of reliable data.
There is a paucity of affordable housing near the campus.

definition: A very large amount of something, often more than is needed.
examples: Shoppers face a plethora of nearly identical phone plans and struggle to choose one.
The festival offered a plethora of workshops, far more than anyone could attend.

definition: To become less strong, or to make something less intense.
examples: After three days the storm finally abated, and the ferries began running again.
The new medicine did nothing to abate the pain in her injured knee.

definition: To choose not to do something you might want to do.
examples: Three members abstained from the vote because they owned shares in the company.
Doctors advised him to abstain from alcohol for a month after the surgery.

definition: To make something poorer in quality by adding a cheaper substance.
examples: The dairy was fined for adulterating its milk with water to increase profits.
Spices adulterated with brick dust were seized from the market by food inspectors.

definition: Relating to beauty or to how pleasing something looks.
examples: The bridge was praised for its aesthetic appeal as much as for its strength.
Her choice of paint was purely aesthetic and had nothing to do with cost.

definition: Cheerful eagerness and speed in doing something.
examples: She accepted the job offer with alacrity, replying within minutes of receiving the email.
The volunteers set to work with such alacrity that the hall was clean by noon.

definition: A strong feeling of dislike toward someone or something.
examples: His antipathy toward paperwork meant that forms sat unopened on his desk for weeks.
The two rivals made no effort to hide their antipathy and refused to shake hands.

definition: A lack of interest, concern or energy about something.
examples: Low turnout at the election was blamed on voter apathy rather than bad weather.
Teachers worried about the apathy of students who no longer bothered to ask questions.

definition: To make an unpleasant feeling less painful or severe.
examples: The manager tried to assuage staff fears by promising that no jobs would be cut.
A glass of cold water did little to assuage his thirst after the race.

definition: Willing to take bold risks that may shock other people.
examples: The audacious thieves stole the painting in daylight while the guards were watching.
It was an audacious plan to cross the desert with only one day's water.

definition: Plain and strict, with no comfort or decoration.
examples: The monks lived in austere rooms furnished with only a bed and a wooden chair.
Her austere father never laughed and allowed no games in the house on weekdays.

definition: To support something and make it stronger.
examples: The new evidence bolstered her argument and convinced the last doubtful members of the jury.
The government cut taxes to bolster the economy during the long slowdown.

definition: To grow or develop very quickly.
examples: The city's burgeoning population has put heavy pressure on its schools and water supply.
Online sales burgeoned during the lockdown, doubling in less than six months.

definition: Honest and direct, even when the truth is unpleasant.
examples: In a candid interview, the actor admitted that he had nearly quit after the film failed.
I want your candid opinion of my essay, not polite praise that hides its faults.

definition: The use of clever tricks to deceive people.
examples: The election was won through chicanery, including forged ballots and bribed officials.
Investors lost millions to the financial chicanery of a director who faked the accounts.

definition: Clearly and logically argued, and therefore convincing.
examples: She gave such a cogent argument for the merger that even its critics agreed.
The lawyer's cogent summary of the evidence persuaded the judge to dismiss the case.

definition: To give evidence that supports a statement or theory.
examples: Two witnesses corroborated his story that he had been at home all evening.
Later experiments corroborated the findings, so the theory gained wide acceptance among physicists.

definition: Extremely cowardly and lacking any courage.
examples: The craven captain abandoned his passengers and took the first lifeboat for himself.
Critics called it a craven decision made only to avoid angering powerful donors.

definition: Polite respect that leads you to accept another person's wishes.
examples: In deference to her grandmother's wishes, the wedding was held in the village temple.
Junior doctors showed such deference to the surgeon that nobody questioned his obvious mistake.

definition: To dry something out completely by removing its moisture.
examples: Months without rain had desiccated the fields, leaving the soil cracked and dusty.
The fruit is desiccated in the sun so that it keeps for a year.

definition: A long, angry speech or piece of writing attacking someone.
examples: The senator launched into a diatribe against the press that lasted nearly an hour.
His review was less a judgment of the book than a bitter diatribe against its author.

definition: Intended to teach, often in a preachy or moralising way.
examples: The novel is too didactic, pausing every few pages to lecture readers about honesty.
Children's stories of that era were openly didactic, each ending with a stated moral.

definition: To spread information or ideas widely among many people.
examples: Health workers disseminated advice about clean water through radio broadcasts and village meetings.
The internet lets anyone disseminate rumours to millions of readers within a few hours.

definition: Made up of things chosen from a wide variety of sources.
examples: Her eclectic taste in music ranges from classical ragas to heavy metal and jazz.
The cafe's eclectic furniture included church pews, school desks and an old barber's chair.

definition: The power of something to produce the result that is wanted.
examples: Trials confirmed the efficacy of the vaccine, which prevented illness in most volunteers.
Researchers doubt the efficacy of the diet because few people lost any weight.

definition: A person or thing that is mysterious and hard to understand.
examples: Even to close friends he remained an enigma who never spoke about his past.
How the ancient builders moved such heavy stones is still an enigma to archaeologists.

definition: To show or declare that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing.
examples: The security footage exculpated the driver by proving he had stopped at the red light.
New DNA evidence exculpated the prisoner after he had spent twelve years in jail.

definition: Careful to spend very little money and waste nothing.
examples: A frugal student, she cooked at home and walked to save the bus fare.
Years of frugal living allowed the couple to buy their house without a loan.

definition: Too ready to believe what other people say; easily tricked.
examples: The gullible tourist paid a stranger fifty dollars for a ticket to a free museum.
Scammers target gullible people with messages promising prizes they never entered to win.

definition: A person who attacks widely accepted beliefs or traditions.
examples: An iconoclast among economists, she argued that the textbook theory of markets was wrong.
The young architect was an iconoclast who mocked the styles his teachers admired.

definition: To make someone less angry by doing what they want.
examples: The airline tried to placate furious passengers with free meals and hotel vouchers.
Nothing would placate the crying child except the return of his lost toy.

definition: To calm someone's anger or soften their hurt feelings.
examples: The minister's apology mollified the protesters, and the crowd slowly began to leave.
She was mollified by his explanation and agreed to give him another chance.

definition: To keep someone calm by giving in to their demands.
examples: The company appeased angry shareholders by replacing the chief executive within a week.
Critics said that trying to appease the dictator with land only encouraged further invasions.

definition: Brief in a way that can seem unfriendly or abrupt.
examples: Her terse reply of 'not now' made it clear she was still annoyed.
The company issued a terse statement of two lines and refused to answer questions.

definition: Expressed clearly in very few words.
examples: Keep your summary succinct, since the committee will only read the first paragraph.
His succinct explanation covered in one minute what the manual took ten pages to say.

definition: Extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy.
examples: The parsimonious owner refused to heat the office even in the middle of winter.
Too parsimonious to buy a ticket, he watched the match through a gap in the fence.

definition: Showing great energy and enthusiasm for a cause or goal.
examples: Zealous supporters queued overnight to hear the candidate speak for only ten minutes.
The new inspector was so zealous that he fined shops for the smallest faults.

definition: Having or showing very strong and sincere feelings.
examples: A fervent believer in free education, she spent her savings building a village school.
The team's fervent fans sang through the entire match despite the heavy rain.

definition: Very enthusiastic or passionate about something.
examples: An ardent admirer of the poet, he had memorised every one of her published works.
She is an ardent defender of wildlife who has campaigned against hunting for decades.

definition: Lacking energy and unwilling to be active.
examples: The heavy lunch left everyone lethargic, and little work was done that afternoon.
After the fever he felt lethargic for days and could barely climb the stairs.

definition: Inactive and slow, as if half asleep.
examples: Snakes become torpid in cold weather and may not move for several weeks.
The torpid economy showed no growth, with shops empty and factories running half shifts.

definition: Habitually lazy and wanting to avoid work.
examples: The indolent clerk spent his mornings reading the newspaper while customers waited in line.
Too indolent to revise, he hoped to pass the exam on luck alone.

definition: Friendly and pleasant in manner; easy to like.
examples: Our amiable host greeted every guest with a smile and a cup of tea.
He was an amiable man whom even his business rivals found hard to dislike.

definition: Describing a relationship or agreement that is friendly and without quarrels.
examples: The couple reached an amicable divorce settlement without ever going to court.
Despite years of competition, the two firms ended their partnership on amicable terms.

definition: Living very simply and refusing comforts, often for religious reasons.
examples: The ascetic monk owned nothing but a robe, a bowl and a blanket.
He led an ascetic life, sleeping on the floor and eating one meal a day.

definition: So satisfied with yourself that you stop trying or noticing danger.
examples: After three easy wins the team grew complacent and lost to the weakest side.
We cannot be complacent about safety just because there has been no accident this year.

definition: Willing to please others and go along with their wishes.
examples: The complaisant waiter changed their order three times without a word of complaint.
Too complaisant to refuse, she agreed to every request her colleagues made of her.

definition: Careful not to attract attention or reveal private information.
examples: A discreet assistant, she never repeated anything she overheard in the director's office.
He made a discreet exit through the side door so nobody would notice him leaving.

definition: Separate and distinct from other things of the same kind.
examples: The course is divided into six discrete units, each with its own exam.
Sound that seems continuous is stored on a disc as millions of discrete samples.

definition: To openly disobey a rule or law without any shame.
examples: Drivers who flout the speed limit near schools now face much heavier fines.
The factory flouted pollution laws for years by dumping waste into the river at night.

definition: To show something off proudly so that others will notice it.
examples: He flaunted his new wealth by parking a different sports car outside each week.
She never flaunts her medals, which stay in a drawer rather than on the wall.

definition: Used so often that it no longer sounds fresh or interesting.
examples: The speech was full of hackneyed phrases like 'think outside the box' and 'win-win'.
Critics complained that the film's hackneyed plot offered no surprise from start to finish.

definition: Control or dominant influence by one group or country over others.
examples: The empire's hegemony over the region lasted two centuries before its neighbours finally rebelled.
Smaller firms struggle against the hegemony of one company that controls most online searches.

definition: An unusual habit or feature that belongs to one particular person.
examples: One of his idiosyncrasies was eating dessert before the main course at every meal.
Her habit of humming while she works is a harmless idiosyncrasy that colleagues enjoy.

definition: Acting quickly and without thinking about the results.
examples: In an impetuous moment he quit his job, and regretted it by the weekend.
The impetuous young driver overtook on a blind corner and nearly caused a crash.

definition: Unable to be calmed, satisfied or made less angry.
examples: She remained an implacable opponent of the dam, rejecting every compromise the builders offered.
His implacable anger toward his brother lasted for decades and survived every attempted apology.

definition: Just begun and so not yet fully formed or clear.
examples: Her plans for the business were still inchoate, little more than a few scribbled notes.
The protesters shared an inchoate sense of anger but had no clear list of demands.

definition: Seeming strange because it does not fit with its surroundings.
examples: The glass skyscraper looked incongruous among the low stone cottages of the old village.
He cut an incongruous figure at the beach, wearing a dark suit and tie.

definition: To try to win someone's favour by flattering or pleasing them.
examples: He tried to ingratiate himself with the new boss by laughing at all her jokes.
The salesman's ingratiating smile vanished as soon as the customer declined to buy.

definition: Not harmful or likely to offend anyone.
examples: The spider looks frightening but is entirely innocuous and cannot bite through human skin.
What seemed an innocuous remark about her cooking somehow started a bitter family argument.

definition: Lacking flavour, interest or energy; dull.
examples: The soup was so insipid that we added salt, pepper and lemon to taste anything.
After the first exciting chapter, the novel sinks into insipid dialogue and predictable romance.

definition: Easily made angry; quick to lose one's temper.
examples: The irascible old editor shouted at reporters for the slightest mistake in their copy.
Lack of sleep made her irascible, and she snapped at anyone who spoke to her.

definition: To place two things side by side to show their differences.
examples: The exhibition juxtaposes photographs of the city's richest and poorest streets to striking effect.
By juxtaposing the two speeches, the article showed how far his views had shifted.

definition: To express deep sadness or regret about something.
examples: Older residents lament the loss of the village shop, which closed after sixty years.
She lamented that she had never learned to swim when the chance was there.

definition: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or a weaker person.
examples: Magnanimous in victory, the champion praised her opponent and shared the prize money with her.
It was magnanimous of him to forgive the friend who had cost him his job.

definition: Easy to shape, change or influence without breaking.
examples: Gold is so malleable that it can be beaten into sheets thinner than paper.
Young children are malleable, absorbing the habits and opinions of the adults around them.

definition: A person who dislikes and avoids other people in general.
examples: A lifelong misanthrope, he lived alone on the island and turned every visitor away.
She is no misanthrope, but after a week of meetings she wanted to see nobody.

definition: Just beginning to exist and starting to develop.
examples: The country's nascent film industry produced only three movies in its first year.
Investors are excited about the nascent technology, although no product has reached the market.

definition: Vague and unclear, without definite shape or limits.
examples: The manager's nebulous promise of 'future rewards' did nothing to satisfy the tired staff.
His plans remained nebulous, with no dates, budget or names attached to any of them.

definition: Displaying wealth or importance in a showy way to impress others.
examples: The ostentatious mansion had gold taps, marble floors and a fountain shaped like a swan.
She disliked ostentatious jewellery and wore only a plain silver ring on her finger.

definition: Strongly supporting one side or party, often without fair judgment.
examples: The partisan crowd booed every decision that went against the home team.
Voters are tired of partisan fighting and want the two parties to cooperate.

definition: Done quickly as a duty, without care or real interest.
examples: The guard gave our bags a perfunctory glance and waved us through without a word.
His apology was so perfunctory that she doubted he felt sorry at all.

definition: Not safe or secure; likely to fall or fail.
examples: The climber clung to a precarious ledge barely wide enough for one foot.
Freelancers live a precarious life, never certain that next month's rent will be covered.

definition: To make something, usually bad, happen suddenly or sooner than expected.
examples: The minister's resignation precipitated a crisis that brought down the government within a week.
A sudden fall in oil prices precipitated the collapse of several small drilling companies.

definition: To increase rapidly in number or spread quickly.
examples: Coffee shops have proliferated in the city centre, with a new one opening every month.
Without predators, the rabbits proliferated until they had eaten most of the island's grass.

definition: Quiet and inactive for a period of time.
examples: The volcano has been quiescent for a century, though scientists still monitor it closely.
After years of protest the movement grew quiescent, holding no rallies and issuing no statements.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to obey rules or follow instructions.
examples: The recalcitrant pupil ignored every warning and was finally sent to the head teacher.
Engineers spent hours coaxing a recalcitrant engine that refused to start in the cold.

definition: To prove that a statement or theory is wrong.
examples: The lawyer refuted the claim by producing a receipt dated the day of the theft.
New fossil discoveries refuted the old theory that the species had died out earlier.

definition: Unwilling to speak freely about one's thoughts or feelings.
examples: He was reticent about his years in the army and changed the subject when asked.
Normally reticent, she surprised everyone by speaking for ten minutes about her childhood.

definition: Tending to make people feel sleepy.
examples: The lecturer's soporific voice had half the class dozing within the first twenty minutes.
Warm milk is said to have a soporific effect when drunk just before bedtime.

definition: More than is needed or wanted; unnecessary.
examples: Cut the superfluous words from your essay so that every sentence earns its place.
With the new software doing the sums, a second accountant became superfluous.

definition: Dishonest behaviour meant to trick people; double-dealing.
examples: His duplicity was exposed when both clients discovered he had promised each the same contract.
She was shocked by the duplicity of a friend who praised her but mocked her privately.

definition: Not telling the truth; given to lying.
examples: The mendacious advertisement claimed the pills cured diseases that they could not even affect.
Reporters exposed the mendacious official by comparing his statements with the actual records.

definition: Disloyal and ready to betray someone's trust.
examples: The perfidious general sold the city's defence plans to the enemy for gold.
She never forgave her perfidious partner, who had secretly emptied their shared bank account.

definition: Fearless and eager for adventure or danger.
examples: The intrepid reporter travelled alone into the war zone to interview the rebel leaders.
Only the most intrepid hikers attempt the icy ridge during the winter months.

definition: Showing courage and never discouraged by danger or difficulty.
examples: The dauntless rescue team kept searching through the storm until every climber was found.
Dauntless despite three failed attempts, she entered the competition again and finally won.

definition: Kept secret or done secretly, often because it is not allowed.
examples: The rebels held clandestine meetings in a cellar to avoid the attention of police.
Their clandestine romance stayed hidden from both families for more than two years.

definition: Done secretly or quickly so that others will not notice.
examples: He took a surreptitious look at his phone under the table during the meeting.
The student made a surreptitious attempt to copy from the paper on the next desk.

definition: Quiet and secretive in a way that suggests guilt.
examples: The boy cast a furtive glance at the door before slipping the sweets into his pocket.
Her furtive behaviour, hiding letters and whispering on the phone, made her parents suspicious.

definition: Causing harm or damage, often in a gradual way.
examples: Years of smoking had a deleterious effect on his lungs and left him short of breath.
The chemical is deleterious to fish, so the factory may not release it into rivers.

definition: Having a very harmful effect that is gradual and hard to notice.
examples: The pernicious rumour spread slowly through the office until nobody trusted the new manager.
Doctors warn about the pernicious influence of advertisements that make junk food appealing to children.

definition: Causing harm or damage to something.
examples: Lack of sleep is detrimental to memory, which is why late revision often fails.
The new road proved detrimental to local shops, since drivers no longer passed through town.

definition: Using more words than are needed.
examples: The verbose contract ran to ninety pages when ten would have covered every point.
His verbose answers bored the interviewers, who wanted a simple yes or no.

definition: To draw out a response, answer or reaction from someone.
examples: The teacher's question failed to elicit a single answer from the silent class.
The comedian's opening joke elicited loud laughter and put the nervous audience at ease.

definition: Not allowed by law or by accepted social rules.
examples: Police seized a lorry carrying illicit cigarettes that had been smuggled across the border.
The minister resigned after reports of illicit payments from a construction company.

definition: Full of twists and turns; long and complicated.
examples: The bus crawled up a tortuous mountain road with a sharp bend every few metres.
After tortuous negotiations lasting three years, the two countries finally signed a trade agreement.

definition: Causing great pain or suffering that is hard to bear.
examples: The runners faced a torturous final mile in blistering heat with no water left.
Waiting a week for the exam results was torturous for the anxious students.

definition: Famous and highly respected, especially within a particular profession.
examples: An eminent surgeon was flown in to perform the delicate operation on the president.
The prize is awarded each year by a panel of eminent scientists and writers.

definition: Likely to happen very soon, used especially of something unpleasant.
examples: Dark clouds and a sudden wind warned the sailors that a storm was imminent.
With the factory's closure imminent, hundreds of workers began searching for new jobs.

definition: To criticise someone severely and officially for something they did.
examples: The council voted to censure the mayor for spending public money on private travel.
The doctor was censured by the medical board for failing to record the treatment.

definition: To remove parts of a book, film or message considered unacceptable.
examples: The government censored the newspaper, deleting every article that criticised the army.
Soldiers' letters home were censored so that no details of troop positions leaked out.

definition: Bitter, angry feeling or speech between people.
examples: The divorce was settled without acrimony, and the couple remained friends for years afterward.
Years of acrimony between the two families ended when their children decided to marry.

definition: To warn or gently scold someone about their behaviour.
examples: The librarian admonished the students for talking loudly while others were trying to read.
She admonished her son to drive slowly on the icy roads that evening.

definition: Something that belongs to a different time from the one shown.
examples: The wristwatch on the Roman soldier was an obvious anachronism in the historical film.
In an age of email, the handwritten ledger seemed a charming anachronism to visitors.

definition: To give a false idea of something; to hide the truth.
examples: Her calm smile belied the panic she felt as she walked onto the stage.
The shop's shabby front belies the quality of the food served inside it.

definition: Using grand, important-sounding words that have little real meaning.
examples: The candidate's bombastic speech promised a glorious new age but offered no actual policies.
Readers soon tire of his bombastic style, with its long words and empty boasts.

definition: A harsh, unpleasant mixture of loud sounds.
examples: A cacophony of car horns, drills and shouting vendors greeted us outside the station.
The orchestra's tuning produced a cacophony that made the children cover their ears.

definition: Careful to consider all risks before acting or speaking.
examples: After losing money once, she became circumspect and researched every company before investing.
The diplomat gave a circumspect answer, anxious not to offend either government.

definition: A confusing problem or question that is difficult to solve.
examples: How to cut costs without losing staff was a conundrum the board could not solve.
Parents face the conundrum of protecting children online while still respecting their privacy.

definition: Deserving blame for something wrong or harmful.
examples: The court found the driver culpable because he had ignored two clear warning signs.
Managers who knew about the leak and stayed silent were equally culpable for the damage.

definition: To mock someone or something as worthless or ridiculous.
examples: Critics derided the plan as a fantasy that no serious engineer would support.
He was derided by classmates for his accent, yet later became a famous actor.

definition: A lack of something; too little of what is needed.
examples: A dearth of rain this summer has left the reservoirs at half their usual level.
The village suffers from a dearth of doctors, with the nearest clinic miles away.

definition: To move away from the main subject while speaking or writing.
examples: The professor often digressed into stories about his travels and never finished the lecture.
Let me digress for a moment to explain how this odd tradition first began.

definition: A lack of agreement or harmony between things, especially sounds or ideas.
examples: There is a clear dissonance between the company's green slogans and its polluting factories.
The composer used dissonance deliberately, making listeners uneasy before the melody finally resolved.

definition: Full of cheerful energy and excitement.
examples: The ebullient crowd sang and danced in the streets after the team's unexpected victory.
She was in an ebullient mood, laughing and hugging everyone after receiving the news.

definition: To try to equal or copy someone you admire.
examples: Young players try to emulate the champion's serve by studying videos of her matches.
He hoped to emulate his mother's success and open a restaurant of his own.

definition: To officially clear someone of blame for a fault or crime.
examples: The inquiry exonerated the pilot, finding that a mechanical fault had caused the crash.
She was fully exonerated when the missing money turned up in the bank's own records.

definition: Treating a serious matter with jokes that are out of place.
examples: His facetious comment about the fire alarm annoyed colleagues who were genuinely frightened.
I was being facetious when I suggested we cancel the exam; please keep studying.

definition: Based on a mistaken belief or faulty reasoning.
examples: The argument is fallacious because it assumes that everything expensive must be good.
It is fallacious to conclude that the medicine works from only two patients' recovery.

definition: Happening by chance, especially lucky chance, and not by plan.
examples: A fortuitous meeting on a train led to the partnership that built the company.
The discovery was fortuitous: the scientist had been looking for something else entirely.

definition: Enjoying the company of other people; sociable.
examples: Gregarious by nature, she knew every neighbour's name within a week of moving in.
He is too gregarious to enjoy working alone in a quiet office all day.

definition: To lecture someone at length in a loud, angry way.
examples: The coach harangued the players for twenty minutes about their lazy performance.
A man stood on a box and harangued passers-by about the evils of taxation.

definition: Not allowing something to pass through; not affected by something.
examples: The coat is impervious to rain, so she stayed dry throughout the long storm.
He seemed impervious to criticism and carried on exactly as before despite the complaints.

definition: Belonging naturally to a particular place; native.
examples: The kangaroo is indigenous to Australia and is found wild nowhere else on earth.
The museum displays tools made by the indigenous peoples who lived here before settlers arrived.

definition: Impossible to stop, prevent or persuade.
examples: The inexorable rise of the sea is slowly swallowing villages along the low coast.
Despite every protest, the inexorable spread of the city continued into the surrounding farmland.

definition: Humour or lightness, especially when it is out of place.
examples: His joke brought a moment of levity to an otherwise tense and gloomy meeting.
The judge warned that levity was inappropriate in a courtroom during a murder trial.

definition: An independent person who refuses to follow the group's usual ways.
examples: A maverick in the party, she often voted against her own leader's proposals.
The director was a maverick who ignored studio rules and filmed everything his own way.

definition: Ordinary and dull, with nothing exciting about it.
examples: After the thrill of the expedition, mundane tasks like washing dishes felt almost unbearable.
Most of a detective's work is mundane, involving paperwork and hours of patient waiting.

definition: Too eager to please or obey someone important.
examples: The obsequious waiter bowed repeatedly and laughed at every remark the wealthy guest made.
She disliked the obsequious junior staff who agreed with whatever the director said.

definition: Seeming to be present or found everywhere.
examples: Mobile phones are now ubiquitous, carried even by children and the very elderly.
The coffee chain has become ubiquitous, with a branch on almost every city corner.

definition: To keep changing between different opinions or decisions.
examples: He vacillated for weeks between the two job offers and nearly lost them both.
Voters grew impatient as the government vacillated over whether to raise the tax.

definition: Extremely generous, especially in giving money or gifts.
examples: A munificent donor paid for the entire new wing of the children's hospital.
The prince was munificent to artists, funding dozens of painters and poets at court.

definition: Kind and wanting to do good for other people.
examples: A benevolent neighbour quietly paid the widow's rent for a year after the funeral.
The charity was founded by a benevolent merchant who wanted every child to read.

definition: Caring about the good of others more than your own.
examples: Her altruistic decision to donate a kidney to a stranger saved the man's life.
Not every gift is altruistic; some donors simply want their names on a building.

definition: Hostile and eager to fight or argue.
examples: The belligerent customer shouted at staff and threatened to smash the shop window.
After two drinks he grew belligerent, picking quarrels with everyone at the table.

definition: Bad-tempered and quick to argue or fight.
examples: The truculent teenager answered every question with a scowl and a muttered insult.
Reporters found the minister truculent, snapping at them and refusing to explain his decision.

definition: Naturally inclined to quarrel or start fights.
examples: The pugnacious little dog barked and lunged at animals three times its size.
Known as a pugnacious debater, she attacked every weak point in her opponent's case.

definition: Shy and lacking confidence in one's own ability.
examples: Too diffident to raise her hand, she rarely shared the answers she knew.
The diffident young author apologised for his book before anyone had even read it.

definition: Easily frightened; nervous and lacking courage.
examples: The timorous child hid behind his mother whenever a stranger entered the room.
A timorous investor, he sold his shares at the first hint of bad news.

definition: Old-fashioned and no longer useful or suitable today.
examples: The office still relies on an antiquated computer system that crashes several times a day.
Many consider the law antiquated, since it was written before cars were even invented.

definition: Belonging to a much earlier period; very old-fashioned.
examples: The poem is full of archaic words like 'thee' and 'thou' that nobody uses now.
The club's archaic rules still banned women from entering through the front door.

definition: No longer used because something newer has replaced it.
examples: Typewriters became obsolete once cheap computers and printers appeared in every office.
The factory closed because its machines were obsolete and too costly to replace.

definition: Said so often that it has lost all force.
examples: The card contained a trite message about every cloud having a silver lining.
His advice to 'follow your dreams' sounded trite to graduates worried about paying rent.

definition: Strongly opposed to something or unwilling to do it.
examples: He is averse to risk and keeps all his savings in a bank account.
She was not averse to hard work, but she refused to work without pay.

definition: Harmful or working against what is wanted.
examples: The match was cancelled because of adverse weather, with heavy snow covering the pitch.
The drug was withdrawn after several patients suffered adverse reactions such as severe rashes.

definition: To forbid something officially, especially by law.
examples: The new law proscribes smoking in restaurants, offices and all other enclosed public places.
Several political groups were proscribed, and their members could be arrested for meeting.

definition: To state officially what should be done or which medicine to take.
examples: The doctor prescribed antibiotics for the infection and told him to rest for a week.
The rules prescribe a uniform of white shirt and black trousers for all staff.

definition: Quick to notice and understand things that are not obvious.
examples: A perspicacious reader will spot the clue hidden in the very first chapter.
The perspicacious manager sensed trouble long before the sales figures began to fall.

definition: Clearly expressed and therefore easy to understand.
examples: Her perspicuous instructions meant that even beginners assembled the machine without a single mistake.
The judge praised the lawyer's perspicuous summary, which made a tangled case seem simple.

definition: To tell or inform someone about something.
examples: Please apprise me of any changes to the schedule before the meeting begins tomorrow.
The captain was apprised of the storm ahead and changed course to avoid it.

definition: To judge the value or quality of something.
examples: A jeweller appraised the ring and told her it was worth far more than expected.
Managers appraise each employee's work once a year before deciding on pay rises.

definition: To leave suddenly and secretly, often to avoid being caught.
examples: The treasurer absconded with the club's savings and was never seen in town again.
Two prisoners absconded during the night by climbing over the unguarded back wall.

definition: An award or expression of praise for an achievement.
examples: The film won every major accolade, including the award for best picture that year.
Being named teacher of the year was the highest accolade of her long career.

definition: The ability to make quick, good judgments in a particular area.
examples: Her business acumen turned a small bakery into a chain of forty profitable shops.
He lacked the political acumen to see that his own allies were plotting against him.

definition: To increase the power, wealth or importance of someone or something.
examples: The king used the war to aggrandize himself, seizing land from his weaker neighbours.
She accused the chairman of aggrandizing his own role while ignoring the team's work.

definition: Widely told as true but probably not true at all.
examples: The story that the scientist discovered gravity under an apple tree is probably apocryphal.
Historians dismiss the apocryphal tale of the general's last words as a later invention.

definition: Needing a great deal of effort and hard work.
examples: After an arduous climb of nine hours, the exhausted team finally reached the summit.
Learning to read music was an arduous process that took her several patient years.

definition: Relating to pleasant, peaceful country life.
examples: They left the noisy city for a bucolic village surrounded by meadows and grazing sheep.
The painting shows a bucolic scene of farmers resting beside a quiet stream.

definition: To stop resisting and accept defeat or the other side's demands.
examples: After a month without food supplies, the surrounded city finally capitulated to the invaders.
The company capitulated to the strikers and agreed to raise wages by ten percent.

definition: Bitterly sarcastic and meant to hurt; also, able to burn skin.
examples: Her caustic review reduced the young author to tears and ended his writing career.
His caustic wit made him feared by colleagues, who dreaded becoming his next target.

definition: To come together and form one larger whole.
examples: Several small protest groups coalesced into a single national movement with one leader.
The scattered droplets on the window slowly coalesced into a stream of running water.

definition: Feeling and showing deep regret for having done wrong.
examples: The contrite driver apologised in tears and offered to pay for all the damage.
She sounded genuinely contrite on the phone, admitting that the mistake was entirely hers.

definition: Too willing to believe things without good evidence.
examples: Credulous viewers sent money to the fortune teller who promised to remove their bad luck.
Only a credulous person would accept that a pill could teach you French overnight.

definition: A division into two parts that are sharply different or opposed.
examples: The essay rejects the dichotomy between work and play, arguing that good jobs combine both.
There is a false dichotomy in claiming we must choose between jobs and clean air.

definition: So different from each other that they cannot easily be compared.
examples: The committee brought together disparate groups, from farmers and bankers to students and priests.
It is hard to draw one conclusion from such disparate studies using different methods.

definition: A feeling of tired boredom because nothing interesting is happening.
examples: After a month of idle holidays, ennui set in and he longed for school.
The wealthy heiress suffered from ennui, finding every party and journey equally dull.

definition: Needing immediate action or attention; urgent.
examples: The exigent situation at the flooded hospital forced doctors to move patients within the hour.
Under such exigent circumstances, the mayor could not wait for the council to vote.

definition: To deny or argue against something that has been said.
examples: Nobody could gainsay the evidence once the video of the robbery was shown in court.
It is hard to gainsay her claim, since every record supports what she says.

definition: Clever but dishonest skill in tricking people.
examples: The fox in the fable uses guile, not strength, to steal the crow's cheese.
Lacking any guile, the honest child told the visitors exactly what her parents had said.

definition: Excessive pride or confidence that leads to a person's downfall.
examples: The chief executive's hubris led him to ignore warnings until the company went bankrupt.
It was hubris to call the ship unsinkable before it had completed a single voyage.

definition: Having very little or no money; habitually poor.
examples: The impecunious student lived on rice and lentils and walked everywhere to save bus fares.
Too impecunious to afford a hotel, the travellers slept on benches in the railway station.

definition: To mock someone publicly using humour or exaggeration.
examples: The cartoonist lampooned the prime minister, drawing him as a clown juggling broken promises.
The comedy show lampoons celebrities by exaggerating their voices, clothes and silliest public statements.

definition: Calm and relaxed, showing no worry or interest.
examples: He tried to look nonchalant, whistling as he walked past the guard with the stolen file.
Her nonchalant shrug at the news of the fire shocked everyone in the room.

definition: Not able to be seen through; hard to understand.
examples: The bathroom window is made of opaque glass so that nobody outside can see in.
The contract's opaque wording left even the lawyers unsure what the company had promised.

definition: A person who is rejected and avoided by a group or society.
examples: After betraying his teammates, he became a pariah whom nobody would sit beside at lunch.
The country was treated as a pariah, banned from trade and international sporting events.

definition: A strong and lasting liking for something.
examples: She has a penchant for spicy food and adds chillies to almost every meal.
His penchant for expensive watches left him with little money for anything more useful.

definition: A remark made so often that it is dull and meaningless.
examples: The coach offered only platitudes like 'give it your best' when the team wanted tactics.
Tired of platitudes about patience, the unemployed workers demanded a real plan from officials.

definition: Giving a good chance of success; favourable.
examples: With interest rates low, it seemed a propitious moment to borrow and expand the business.
Clear skies and calm seas were propitious signs for the fishermen setting out at dawn.

definition: Full of noble ideas that are impractical and unlikely to succeed.
examples: His quixotic plan to end poverty by giving away his small salary helped almost nobody.
Friends admired her quixotic campaign to save the old theatre but doubted it could succeed.

definition: Mocking in a bitter, scornful way.
examples: With a sardonic smile, she congratulated him on finally arriving only two hours late.
His sardonic remarks about the boss's 'brilliant' ideas amused colleagues but cost him promotion.

definition: Very weak, thin or slight, and easily broken.
examples: The link between the suspect and the crime was tenuous, resting on one blurred photograph.
The party kept a tenuous hold on power with a majority of just one seat.

definition: Proud in a way that shows contempt for other people.
examples: The haughty duchess refused to speak to servants and looked past them as furniture.
His haughty tone suggested that our questions were far too foolish to deserve answers.

definition: Behaving as if you are better than everyone else.
examples: The supercilious waiter raised an eyebrow when we asked for the cheapest wine.
She gave a supercilious laugh at his accent, as though only her own were correct.

definition: Giving orders in a proud way that expects instant obedience.
examples: With an imperious wave of her hand, the director dismissed the assistants from the room.
His imperious manner annoyed the staff, who disliked being ordered about without a 'please'.

definition: Holding firmly to a goal and refusing to give up.
examples: The tenacious reporter kept asking questions for two years until the truth finally emerged.
She is a tenacious player who chases every ball, even when the match seems lost.

definition: Stubbornly continuing with an opinion or course of action.
examples: The pertinacious salesman returned every morning for a month until the owner finally bought.
Her pertinacious questioning wore down the witness, who at last admitted what he had seen.

definition: Calm and peaceful, and not easily upset.
examples: The placid old horse stood still while small children climbed all over its back.
On a windless morning the lake was so placid that it reflected every cloud.

definition: Peaceful and untroubled, with no sign of worry.
examples: She looked serene throughout the crisis, calmly giving instructions while others around her panicked.
The monastery garden was serene, its silence broken only by birdsong and running water.

definition: Calmness of mind, especially in a difficult situation.
examples: He accepted the loss of his job with equanimity and began searching the next morning.
Nurses must face emergencies with equanimity, since panic would only frighten the patients further.

definition: Gloomy, bad-tempered and unwilling to talk.
examples: After losing the final, the morose captain sat alone and refused to speak to reporters.
He grew morose in winter, staring out of the window and answering in grunts.

definition: Looking or sounding very sad and gloomy, often in an exaggerated way.
examples: The lugubrious music at the funeral made even the strangers in the church weep.
With his long face and lugubrious voice, the actor was always cast as an undertaker.

definition: Sad in a quiet, thoughtful way that lasts a while.
examples: The empty playground in the rain gave the whole street a melancholy air.
She felt melancholy every autumn, remembering the friends who had left the town.

definition: Showing or expressing great sadness; mournful in manner.
examples: The dog gave a doleful howl each time its owner left for work.
He turned his doleful eyes toward the door, hoping she would come back.

definition: To mention something indirectly, without naming it openly.
examples: In her speech she alluded to the scandal without ever mentioning the minister's name.
The poem alludes to an ancient myth that most modern readers no longer recognise.

definition: To escape from or avoid someone or something, often by skill.
examples: The thief eluded the police for months by changing his address every few days.
The answer to the final puzzle eluded her despite an hour of careful thought.

definition: To annoy someone very much, especially by repeated behaviour.
examples: The constant delays exasperated passengers, some of whom had waited at the gate since dawn.
She was exasperated by her brother's habit of borrowing things and never returning them.

definition: Having more than one possible meaning, and therefore unclear.
examples: The sign's ambiguous wording left drivers unsure whether parking was allowed on Sundays.
His ambiguous reply could have meant either yes or no, so we asked again.

definition: Able to be believed or trusted; convincing.
examples: The witness was credible because her account matched the camera footage in every detail.
Without any evidence, his excuse for missing the deadline was simply not credible.

definition: Good enough to deserve praise, though not outstanding.
examples: The young team gave a creditable performance, losing narrowly to last year's champions.
She finished in a creditable fourth place after only six months of training.

definition: Impatient and hard to control because of boredom or delay.
examples: The crowd grew restive as the concert was delayed for a second hour.
Restive after weeks indoors, the children were desperate to run about in the garden.

definition: Having a very unpleasant smell; disgusting or harmful.
examples: A noisome smell rose from the blocked drain and drove customers out of the cafe.
Workers wore masks against the noisome fumes that drifted from the chemical waste pit.
